title: Live versus online jam and how she runs the sign-up list
summary: She would like both formats; she explains calling players up one by one, the closing blues jam, and thinks about an online version.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well congratulations. I’m amazed that people, the ingenuity that is happening, and I’m starting to wonder if when — we’re going to assume that someday we’re going to be back to normal, if things will return to where they were, or, in your case you’re talking about this has been a positive thing, might you end up doing both a live jam and an online jam.

It depends I guess on the budget, but that would be great. I would love to. We need more time every month. We’d never have enough time for all the players. I mean it’s always a stress for me to try to fit everyone in on the evening. I try to call them up one at a time rather than two or three at a time you know, and give them a chance — in the live session.
I’m not sure what you mean, calling them up.

Okay so I mean when they come in and sign the sign-up list in the live jam, there might be 32 players and we only have short of three hours. So some jam sessions call up two or three players at a time to play with the house band. But I try to call them up one by one unless they’re a set group. You know what I mean?

Okay. So it takes some time and we usually can just barely fit everyone in. At the end we usually have a big jam number, like a blues or something, where everybody gets up and sings or plays, and it’s really sweet. I thought that up. I’m trying to think if there’s a way to do that online you know, have everybody do one chorus of the blues and pass it from
one to the other, but I’m not sure if everybody could stay in the same key that way and stuff. Maybe. I’m working on it.
